opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, because "world model" gets used in a lot of different ways. The way I think about it, a world model is something that lets you predict how the world will evolve in response to actions. It's not just predicting the next frame of a video; it's answering, "If I do this, what happens next?" That action-conditioning is really the core of it.

What made Genie interesting to us is that we learned that kind of model purely from video, without any action labels. Most of the internet's video, like people playing 2D platformer games, doesn't come with the controller inputs attached. So a big part of the work was figuring out how to infer actions from unlabeled video. We trained a latent action model that looks at consecutive frames and learns a small, discrete set of latent actions that explain the changes between them. Then the dynamics model learns to predict the next frame given the past frames and one of those latent actions.

Once you have that, you can sit down and actually play it. You press one of those latent actions, and the model generates what happens next, frame by frame. And what was really exciting is that the latent actions ended up being consistent and semantically meaningful. One of them would reliably mean something like "move left" or "jump" across very different environments, even though we never told the model what those actions were.

So for me, what makes Genie a world model is that combination: it's interactive and controllable, it captures something about how the environment responds to an agent, and it learned all of that from passive observation. You could even give it an image it had never seen, like a sketch someone drew, and turn it into a playable world. That points toward a future where we could generate an essentially unlimited variety of environments, which matters a lot for training more general agents.

r001.rationale: The response says Genie is interactive and controllable: an agent can press a latent action and the model generates what happens next.

r002.rationale: It mentions 2D platformer videos and says latent actions work across different environments, but does not clearly identify generalizing across 2D platformer games as Genie’s aim.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it, a world model is really something that lets you imagine what happens next in an environment given some action you take. So you have a state of the world, you take an action, and the model predicts how the world changes in response. That's the core idea, and it's been a big part of model-based reinforcement learning for a long time, where you learn a model of the environment and then use it to plan or to train an agent inside of it instead of interacting with the real thing.

What makes Genie a world model, and what I think is kind of exciting about it, is that it does this but it learns entirely from video. We didn't have any action labels. We just took a huge amount of internet video, mostly of 2D platformer games, and the model had to figure out on its own that there's some latent notion of action that explains how one frame turns into the next. So we have this latent action model that infers, essentially, "what happened between these two frames," and it compresses that into a small discrete set of actions, like eight of them. And then there's a dynamics model that, given the current frame and one of those latent actions, predicts the next frame.

So you end up with something that's controllable. You can give it a single image, even a sketch or a photo, and then you can step through it action by action and it generates a consistent, playable world. That interactivity is really the thing that separates it from just a video generation model. A video model gives you a clip. A world model gives you something you can act in, where your choices actually change what comes next. And for us, the interesting part is that those actions emerged without anyone ever telling the model what "jump" or "move left" means. It discovered that structure from the data, and the actions ended up being pretty consistent across different games and even across images that look nothing like what it was trained on.

r001.rationale: The response describes a world model as predicting how the world changes after an action and says Genie produces a controllable, playable world that responds to actions.

r002.rationale: It says Genie learned from video mostly of 2D platformer games and that its inferred actions were consistent across different games, communicating generalization across games.

astra-6.text:
I think of a world model as something that learns how an environment evolves and how an agent’s actions affect that environment. Genie fits that description because it doesn’t just generate a video that you watch—you can interact with it. You give it an action, and it generates what happens next, conditioned on that action and what’s happened so far.

The interesting part is that it learns from video without needing labels telling it which actions were taken. It learns a latent action space that captures changes between frames, and you can then use those actions to control the generated environment. So it’s learning both how to represent the world and something about its dynamics. That doesn’t mean it’s a perfect simulator, but it gives you a model you can act within.

r001.rationale: It describes an environment an agent can interact with by giving actions, which determine what happens next.

r002.rationale: It discusses Genie learning from video and latent actions, but does not state that its aim is to generalize across 2D platformer games.

sol-6.1.text: I think of a world model as a model that learns how an environment works—how it changes over time and how actions influence those changes. Genie learns that from video, without being given explicit action labels. It learns a latent action space that captures ways the world can change, and then uses those actions to generate what happens next. So you can start with an image and interact with the environment it generates. That action-conditioned prediction is what makes it a world model, rather than simply a model that generates a video you passively watch.

r001.rationale: The response describes an environment that can be interacted with through actions, which influence how it changes.
